The Women's World Cup is coming home... but 2035 cannot be treated as a fix for the game's problems, writes TARA ANSON-WALSH

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 14:36 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:04 EST, 23 November 2026.
  • The United Kingdom will host the 2035 Women's World Cup, the first football World Cup to be staged on these shores since 1966, it was revealed to much fanfare on Monday.
  • Yet while the countdown can now officially begin, the biggest challenges facing the women's game cannot be kicked eight-and-a-half years down the road.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By TARA ANSON-WALSH, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 14:36 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:04 EST, 23 November 2026.

The United Kingdom will host the 2035 Women's World Cup, the first football World Cup to be staged on these shores since 1966, it was revealed to much fanfare on Monday.

Yet while the countdown can now officially begin, the biggest challenges facing the women's game cannot be kicked eight-and-a-half years down the road.

Over in Zurich, FIFA president Gianni Infantino undertook his usual long-winded and self-serving monologue which precedes these ceremonies, in which he heralded the 'incredible growth' of the Women's World Cup, describing a time when they 'didn't exist'.

'We all remember the last Women's World Cup,' the embattled 56-year-old Italian said, calling it 'a huge success'.

The irony, of course, is that the last Women's World Cup in Australia and Latest Zealand is remembered by many for all the wrong reasons, with newspaper back pages peppered with images of Spain captain Jenni Hermoso's kiss with the former president of Spain's FA, Luis Rubiales, for days after the final.

Rubiales was later convicted of sexual assault for the incident, which triggered widespread protests across the country and overshadowed Spain's terrific 1-0 triumph over England in Sydney.

Gianni Infantino undertook his usual long-winded and self-serving monologue which precedes these ceremonies, in which he heralded the 'incredible growth' of the Women's World Cup.

Rubiales was later convicted of sexual assault for the incident, which triggered widespread protests across the country and overshadowed Spain's terrific 1-0 triumph over England.

There is an added layer of irony in that Infantino had, two days before the 2023 final, angered many women worldwide with yet another controversial speech in which he told them: 'You have the power to change', but that they had to 'convince us men what we have to do'.

Alongside this patronising statement, Infantino also insisted that equal pay at the World Cup 'would not solve anything'.

Three years later, Infantino is unfortunately still at the helm, while UEFA's attempts to unseat him following his controversial bid to sell off the World Cup now look to have failed spectacularly, with the football despot increasingly likely to secure a fourth term.

Recent findings suggest that what the social and political landscape will look like by the time this women's footballing bonanza arrives on these shores in 2035 remains unclear. What is clear, however, is that the game's continued progress will require more than the record attendances and soaring commercial revenues the FA are predicting.

It will require the figures who have too often held it back to finally step aside, and that process should begin with the likes of Infantino being shown the door.

It will require those at the top of English football to put their heads together and work out how to stem falling attendances in the league. The average attendance across the first eight WSL matchweeks of 2024-25 was 8,173. Last season it was 7,472. This season, it is tracking at around 5,677.

And third, it will require somewhere other than Wembley to stage the final.

Wembley was, of course, the scene of Chloe Kelly's moment of madness, yet by the time the 2035 Women's World Cup comes around it will also have hosted the men's finals of Euro 2024 and 2028.

The FA paid off its debt on the national stadium in 2024, 17 years after its reopening, and is no longer obligated to host major events there to service repayments.

The rules have been left open for another venue to emerge to host the final, such as Man United's proposed upcoming 100,000 stadium.

While under current FIFA regulations, Wembley is the only one of the proposed 22 stadiums that meets the requirements to host a final, the rules have been left open enough for another venue to emerge should a suitable stadium be completed before 2035.

Step up Sir Jim Ratcliffe, although please refer back to point one in this regard – the Manchester United co-owner who famously asked former captain Katie Zelem 'what do you do here?' while touring the club's women's facilities.

United's proposed upcoming 100,000-seater stadium was included in the 2035 bid and could yet come under consideration from FIFA.

While there are still many hurdles to clear before then, hosting a tournament final in Manchester would undoubtedly be huge for the women's game, not least given the optics of a bid built around being 'all together', described as 'a rallying cry to unite people through football'.

London should not be the epicentre of the tournament, not if the intention is to spread the women's game across the United Kingdom rather than concentrate it in the capital, where Arsenal's attendances continue to dwarf those of every other WSL club.

In other words, the women's game in this country cannot be put on hold until 2035.

In a recent development, it cannot afford to wait eight-and-a-half years for this World Cup to come and rescue it. Time to get cracking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius mentioned ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who remarked Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war.".

The German defense minister remarked "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing.".

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts.".

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel.".

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over concerns tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she quickly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk said he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges.".

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights.".

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl mentioned on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

Industry observers note that france was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC mentioned that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

It has been revealed that "The ball is now in the employer's court," VC mentioned in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, stated it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also mentioned arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

Industry observers note that the ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, mentioned the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger stated the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, confirmed plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl noted on Tuesday that the looks would end in a "shipwreck.".

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support.".

In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it stated.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the intends, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's intends are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he remarked.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he mentioned, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals.".

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The initiative to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius declared on Tuesday.

He mentioned that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the upcoming funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He noted Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has remarked he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He mentioned Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents.".

It also stated that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank.".

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission remarked stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the initiative, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law.".

Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

Breaking: Gianni Infantino’s controversial World Cup sell-off strategy was ‘set to run for 96 years’

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A controversial proposal proposed by Gianni Infantino to establish Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) would have transferred commercial rights for the World Cup for up to 96 years, according to leaked documents.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A controversial proposal proposed by Gianni Infantino to establish Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) would have transferred commercial rights for the World Cup for up to 96 years, according to leaked documents.

First revealed in a report by The Times on 28 July, the project – which involved private investors taking a minority stake – was dropped by Infantino on 1 August following opposition from three continental confederations.

Fifa had previously confirmed in July that the private investment group was to be led by Thrive Capital, a firm established by Joshua Kushner, the brother of United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

Reports published on Monday by The Guardian and the New York Post cited leaked files showing that all commercial rights for Fifa competitions would have been handed to FFE for commercial exploitation over a 96-year period.

The Guardian reported that the contract was structured on a rolling basis up to a maximum of 96 years, with the Fresh York Post adding that only a severe contract breach by FFE could terminate the agreement.

Both outlets reported details of an FFE management bonus pool, which could have awarded $50 million (£38.3m) for every $1 billion added to the initial $20bn valuation of the business.

The files also indicated that the board of FFE was to be chaired by the sitting Fifa president, a position presently held by Infantino.

A Fifa spokesperson mentioned: "Fifa has consistently stated that the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal would have been subject to the approval of the Fifa Member Associations and the Fifa Council.

Sources indicate that "For the avoidance of doubt, any potential Management Incentive Plan was exclusively for members of FFE management, of which Fifa officials could not have been part. This is customary for proposed structures of this nature.

"Fifa’s leadership would only have had leading roles in the board, which would not have led to any additional remuneration. The remuneration of the Fifa President is set by the independent compensation sub-committee.

"Fifa intends to reply to questions submitted by its Council members and has no intention of breaching confidentiality by commenting first to media.".

Fifa has invited Council members to review files relating to FFE at its Zurich headquarters.

Football Association chair and Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt intends to accept, though she and other European representatives on the Council are seeking clarity regarding which documents will be available, the review protocols, and non-disclosure terms.

Meanwhile, Uefa has lodged applications in the US legal system seeking document disclosure from Fifa, Thrive, and advising bank JP Morgan, with a view to possible Swiss criminal proceedings.

Fifa has described Uefa’s court filings as a "smear campaign".

Uefa stated in August that it had "lost confidence" in Infantino over the FFE proposal and has backed French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo to challenge the Swiss official in next year’s election.

However, Infantino remains the firm favourite to win a fourth term at the Fifa Congress in Rabat, Morocco next March.

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020.

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s fair to say that anyone would be spoilt for choice when it comes to selecting the most physical challenge of Graeme Souness’ career.

The fiery Scot was one of the most uncompromising players of his - or anyone else’s - generation, with the former Liverpool skipper taking no prisoners as he patrolled the middle of the park.

Sources indicate that but even by his standards, one challenge stands out above all. That came in a European Cup tie against Steaua Bucharest in 1987, when Liverpool welcomed the Romanian side back to Anfield.

According to recent reports, “We'd gone out there and lost the first leg 2-0,” Souness recalls to FourFourTwo. “There was a guy called Marius Lacatus who was going around topping people.

“In the second game, I thought, ‘If I get half a chance, I'll give him one.’”.

It didn’t take long for that chance to present itself.

“After about 10 minutes, I went through this guy at groin height – when he went down and rolled over, I thought, ‘I've got the wrong player…' Lacatus was 15 or 20 yards away, laughing at me because he thought I was getting sent off.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Much to Souness’ surprise, that red card didn’t come.

“When I made the challenge, I thought, ‘F**k, I've got a problem here', so I went down as well, pretending someone had kicked me. It worked! I should have been arrested and spent time behind bars…”.

The Scot would recieve his fair share of red and yellow cards during his illustrious playing career, but as he looks back on his career, he does not regret this approach.

Sources indicate that “The reality is that I was sent off six or seven times in my career,” he continues. “Not bad given the nature of the game in those days. Every team had a couple of people who would get involved in the physical aspect.

“At Liverpool, people didn't say, ‘Oh we're playing Liverpool today, let's have a jolly nice game of football.' It was, ‘Let's put a few of them on their backsides and see how they deal with it.' If you stood up to that and it settled into a game of football, generally we'd win.

“We could do both – we had to.”.

Graeme Souness' fresh book My Rangers is available now.

Sources indicate that for more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 14:08 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:56 EST, 23 November 2026.

Jack Grealish returned to the Everton squad for the first time since being made unavailable for selection due to a breach of club discipline, and came off the bench at half-time against Brentford on Monday.

It has been revealed that the Manchester City loanee was punished by the club for failing to report to training sessions and missed several matches. He had not featured for four games: one because of illness, then a 'breach of club discipline' and a lack of fitness thereafter.

He last featured on October 17, over a month ago, but returned to the match day squad to take on Brentford on Monday night – named on the substitutes' bench. He was introduced at half-time for Tyrique George, with the Toffees 2-0 down and down to 10 men after James Tarkowski's red card. They would ultimately lose 4-0.

Manager David Moyes said ahead of the game: 'He has served his punishment and we will treat him as we were treating him before.

'We will get on with things. The team is going really well at the moment and what I don't want to do is turn it into a Jack story because it shouldn't be.'.

Sources indicate that pushed if that suggests he will not play on Monday night, Moyes replied: 'He could easily. He is back in the squad, he is a good player. Who knows?'.

Jack Grealish (right) returned to Everton action on Monday for the first time since being punished for missing training.

He was named on the bench against Brentford, coming on for Tyrique George at half-time.

Sources indicate that everton had won their last three games and went into Monday's match sixth in the table. The result, though, was a blow as they dropped to ninth.

In a recent development, asked what Grealish can offer, Moyes added: 'Jack can offer us a lot. I want more from him, I want him to show more than he has done. I want him to give me more assists, goals.

'But there's lots of things about him which we need and he's good at retaining the ball, giving us good possession, carrying. So we hope that he can get back to those levels and give us what we need.

'I think this time last year he was probably sitting on five or six assists so we're hoping to get that.'.

Grealish's social media apology came after he featured in a behind-closed-doors match during the international break.

According to recent reports, 'Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training!' Grealish wrote. 'I want to apologise to the fans (and) everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.

'I love playing for this club (and) can't wait to be back playing in front of you guys in an Everton shirt.

'See you all soon (blue heart emoji)'.

A cyber attack has compromised personal data stored on a LaLiga digital platform, Spain's top football league confirmed in an official statement on Monday.

The precise scale of the breach, which occurred between 14 and 16 November, remains unknown. However, LaLiga stated that personal data from both a fan platform and individual football clubs were affected during the incident.

The matter has been escalated to the Spanish Agency for the Protection of Data, as well as reported to the National Police's Central Unit of Cyber-Delinquency.

LaLiga discovered the cyber incident on 16 November and immediately implemented measures to contain it.

The organisation's IT security personnel are right now evaluating platform logs to determine which specific data was compromised, while monitoring across all online systems has been stepped up to prevent further security breaches.

A number of cyber attacks have taken place across the globe in recent weeks, with the European Union (EU) confirming it had been targeted last week.

An official said cyber security specialists had been responding to an artificial intelligence-generated attack on a key EU institution for almost a month, leaving a number of the bloc's digital systems offline.

The official offered no further details on the nature of the breach or who might be responsible. It represents the first instance of the 27-member union disclosing a cyberattack carried out using an AI tool.

"AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities," mentioned Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive branch of the 27-nation EU.

"Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools," he added. "We have seen many global cyber attacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.".

Sources indicate that regnier noted that the EU initially detected the security incident on 22 October. Officials immediately opened an investigation while implementing "preventative measures.".

According to recent reports, the incident was first reported by news website Politico, which stated the breach lasted for at least 10 days and impacted systems used for translation, reimbursement, salaries and timesheets. Regnier declined to confirm that report.

In a recent development, "We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier noted. So far, he added, "we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole.".

Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace organization Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
  • The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
  • According to recent reports, "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace organization Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

According to recent reports, "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business.".

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the manufacturer is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments.".

Airbus and the US firm Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

She notes because the matter is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she remarked.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

Recent findings suggest that "The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors.".

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, states the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential glitch is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak indicates it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she noted. "That remains to be seen.".

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

It has been revealed that "The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things.".

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

Sources indicate that "Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously.".

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' strategy to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce.".

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

According to recent reports, "I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak noted. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union.".

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

Sources indicate that "We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he remarked. "That in itself is an escalatory development.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League.
  • Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.
  • This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League.

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

Marlon Gomes (Shakhtar Donetsk).

Josko Gvardiol (Manchester City).

Matheus Cunha* (Manchester United).

Alessandro Bastoni* (Inter Milan).

Cristian Martinez (Slovan Bratislava).

Alexis Mac Allister (Liverpool).

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card.

Why Manchester United will surpass Liverpool’s title drought

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “My greatest challenge was knocking Liverpool right off their f****** perch.”.
  • Sir Alex Ferguson’s famous quote has become so embedded in football folklore that its provenance is often misremembered.
  • The then-Manchester United manager did not deliver the emphatic line in the early years of his tenure, as is sometimes claimed, but during a poor run of form in September 2002.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“My greatest challenge was knocking Liverpool right off their f****** perch.”.

Sir Alex Ferguson’s famous quote has become so embedded in football folklore that its provenance is often misremembered.

The then-Manchester United manager did not deliver the emphatic line in the early years of his tenure, as is sometimes claimed, but during a poor run of form in September 2002. The Red Devils had won seven of the previous 10 Premier League crowns, while Liverpool were not even halfway through their 30-year title drought.

Ferguson uttered that comment during Liverpool’s 13th successive campaign without winning the top flight. Fast forward almost a quarter of a century, and United are 13 years into a decline that set in as soon as the Scot retired.

Sources indicate that the Red Devils’ title drought is already nearly half as long as the one Liverpool experienced between 1990 and 2020. They are in the Premier League relegation zone ahead of today’s trip to Anfield, so we can safely say their wait will stretch to at least the 2027/28 season, which will be 15 years since they last won the top flight.

Clearly, the 30-year mark is still a long way off and plenty can happen in that time. But it is also undeniable that United are as far from title challengers as they have been since 2013 and there are no signs of that changing.

In a recent development, that starts from the top. In September, executive co-chairman Avram Glazer told Deutsche Bank’s Sports Investment Conference in London that clubs of United’s stature are not dependent on success on the pitch for commercial power. The quotes, first reported by The Athletic, emerged this month when the Red Devils were about to sack manager Michael Carrick following their slide down the table.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Glazer’s comments were strikingly similar to those of former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward in May 2018, when he told shareholders: “Playing performance doesn’t really have a meaningful impact on what we can do on the commercial side of the business.”.

The fact that those two quotes occurred eight-and-a-half years apart suggests that as long as the Glazer family remain United’s majority owners, the club will prioritise commercial gain over on-pitch success.

It has been revealed that the Americans also appear to be in no rush to sell their majority stake in the club, despite being universally unpopular with the fanbase. A report from TEAMtalk last week claimed they are unlikely to step away until United’s proposed 100,000-capacity stadium is built - which may not be until 2035 - in order to extract maximum value from their investment.

Other outlets claim the Glazers could be interested in selling their stake to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe before then, but that certainly would not guarantee success, with the British businessman’s record in football across United, French club Nice and Swiss outfit Lausanne-Sport patchy at best.

When Ratcliffe bought a minority stake in the club in February 2024, taking control of sporting operations, it was supposed to end a decade of managerial mis-steps and overpaying for underperforming players.

However, the situation has deteriorated further, with chief executive officer Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox facing heavy criticism from fans. The Red Devils finished 15th in 2024/25 and have won just one league game this term, while the one positive half-season of the Ratcliffe era came when Carrick took over as interim boss from Ruben Amorim - another failed appointment - in January and overperformed expectations by qualifying for the Champions League.

Ultimately, United will not become a force again without an ownership change. As the Manchester United Supporters Trust (MUST) said in its statement following Carrick’s sacking: “Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.”.

According to recent reports, this is where Liverpool’s title drought is instructive. Part of the reason for the Reds’ decline in the 1990s and 2000s was because they were overtaken financially by their rivals - initially Ferguson’s United, then Chelsea following Roman Abramovich’s takeover - under their long-time owners, the Moores family.

According to recent reports, after the chaotic ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett, Fenway Sports Group (FSG) bought Liverpool in 2010. FSG did not get it right immediately, but after appointing Jurgen Klopp as manager in 2015 and putting the right people in key positions, such as sporting director Michael Edwards, the Reds were able to challenge regularly for the biggest honours again.

The team that won the title in 2020 featured some big-money recruits, most notably Virgil van Dijk and Alisson, but also several cheaper signings that resulted from a recruitment overhaul, such as Mo Salah, Roberto Firmino and Andy Robertson.

But the key point is that it took Liverpool 10 years of FSG ownership to end their title drought, and only once every department at the club, from the owners to the recruitment team to Klopp, were aligned in pursuit of on-pitch success.

Sources indicate that it is why upcoming United manager Mauricio Pochettino can only do so much. Like Carrick last season, Erik ten Hag in 2022/23 or Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2020/21, there may well be good spells during his tenure, but to paraphrase MUST, the head coach at Old Trafford will inevitably be undermined by the owners sooner or later.

Even when the Glazers eventually sell, we cannot expect the club to immediately become the force they once were, as the Liverpool example demonstrates. It takes time to return to the top when you have been also-rans for so long.

That is why it is easy to see how United’s title drought could stretch beyond 30 years, as hypothetical as that sounds right now. If the Glazers stay in charge for the foreseeable future, the new owners would need time to undo the damage and put everything in place for success. Only then could United start to consistently challenge for the title and there is no guarantee they would win it straight away.

This scenario would have seemed unthinkable when Ferguson made his famous quip in 2002, but when you fall off your perch it is difficult to get back up - as Liverpool know all too well.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many early-career mathematicians are concerned about how AI models will affect their career prospects.Credit: Getty.
  • AI company Anthropic has claimed to have proved the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most famous open problem in mathematics — with the help of its model Claude.
  • Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many early-career mathematicians are concerned about how AI models will affect their career prospects.Credit: Getty.

AI company Anthropic has claimed to have proved the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most famous open problem in mathematics — with the help of its model Claude. The proposed proof, which is still being scrutinized, is the latest in a series of spectacular AI advances in mathematics that are upending the field.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

But the technology’s rapid progress is making early-career mathematicians anxious about the impact that it will have on their futures, according to two studies released in October.

Industry observers note that one was a survey of graduate students and postdocs1 designed by three PhD students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge and uploaded to the preprint server arXiv. The other was conducted by the Martingale Foundation, a non-profit organization in London that supports postgraduate students. It surveyed people at all career stages, but the respondents were limited to UK mathematicians.

Key concerns included job security and feelings of demotivation — 70% of respondents to the student-led survey noted that they were now more likely to consider careers outside academia.

Many mathematicians interviewed by Nature say that the survey results match what they have been hearing from their peers. Graduate students, in particular, feel that they need to develop their own skills and prove their worth at solving mathematical problems without AI. Some are also concerned about the long-term availability of academic jobs — and whether hard-won results produced by their human reasoning could be put them at a disadvantage in a job market where others use AI.

Source: Martindale Foundation report Mathematics in the Age of AI: The Impact on Postgraduate Experience.

“The younger generation seems much more sceptical,” indicates Tasmin Chu, a mathematics PhD student at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. “Fundamentally, that’s because they are in a much worse material position.”.

The student-led survey found that only around 7% of the 268 voluntary respondents — most of whom were at US institutions — felt that AI developments would make it easier for them to get a job that would lead to an eventual professorship. Meanwhile, more than 75% of people expected it to become harder.

Only 13% of respondents stated that they were letting AI tools produce papers for them from start to finish, although a majority of people said that they were using the tools for literature searches or finding mistakes in their papers. Of those respondents who do use AI tools, more than half said that they dislike doing so, and only around 30% said that they enjoy using them. More than three-quarters of respondents said that they would be unhappy if an AI model were to solve a problem that they had worked on (see ‘Pride in discovery’).

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03795-5.

Brandenberger, A., Mularczyk, H. & Woodruff, D. Preprint at arXiv https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.40584 (2026).

The Women’s World Cup is coming to the UK – but what will it look like?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • The United Kingdom has been confirmed as the hosts of the 2035 Women’s World Cup, in what is set to be the largest single-sport event ever to be staged in the country.
  • The joint “All Together” bid from the football associations of the four home nations – England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland – was approved by acclamation and officially confirmed during an online meeting of the Fifa Congress on Monday, although it was the only bidder in the process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The United Kingdom has been confirmed as the hosts of the 2035 Women’s World Cup, in what is set to be the largest single-sport event ever to be staged in the country.

The joint “All Together” bid from the football associations of the four home nations – England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland – was approved by acclamation and officially confirmed during an online meeting of the Fifa Congress on Monday, although it was the only bidder in the process.

The tournament will nevertheless be the first Women’s World Cup to be staged in the UK, as well as the first football World Cup to be held in the UK since England hosted the men’s World Cup in 1966.

Although the UK will be hosting the men’s Euros in 2028, the 2035 Women’s World Cup will be twice the size in terms of competition format: with 48 teams playing 104 matches across a period of five weeks, and around 4.5 million tickets set to be available for fans.

It also promises to build on the legacy of the Lionesses, who won the Euros at Wembley in 2022 and have played in three consecutive major tournament finals – also reaching the Women’s World Cup final in 2023 and retaining the Euros in 2025.

“On behalf of the Football Associations of England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, thank you for your trust and confidence in awarding us the Fifa Women’s World Cup 2035,” FA chair Debbie Jevans stated following the confirmation.

According to recent reports, “We’re deeply honoured by your support, and grateful for the opportunity to host the pinnacle of women’s football on behalf of the global football family. Together, we will celebrate the power of women’s football, inspire the next generation and unite fans from every corner of the world.

“We look forward to welcoming you to the United Kingdom in 2035 and to deliver an exceptional Fifa Women’s World Cup that the entire football community can be proud of.”.

It has been revealed that the Women’s World Cup only expanded to 32 teams ahead of the tournament in Australia and Latest Zealand in 2023; by 2031, it will expand to 48 teams – matching the format of the men’s World Cup – for the tournament in the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica. The competition will have doubled in size in the space of 16 years.

In a recent development, with such a strong portfolio of existing stadiums across the country, the UK’s bid “significantly exceeded” the minimum requirement of 14 venues. The original proposal includes 16 stadiums in England, three in Wales, two in Scotland and one in Northern Ireland, and some that have yet to be built.

Manchester United have signalled their ambition to host the 2035 Women’s World Cup final in their planned new 100,000-capacity stadium. But United’s timeline around the construction of the new £2bn stadium, or who is going to pay for it, remains ambiguous, so the current Old Trafford was included in the UK’s bid as well.

Sources indicate that if the new stadium is built in time, it could mean the Women’s World Cup final is held outside London, with Wembley previously hosting the men’s World Cup final in 1966 as well as men’s and women’s Euros finals in 1996, 2021, 2022 and 2028. Prime minister Andy Burnham said he wanted Manchester to host the final when he was previously mayor of the city.

Recent findings suggest that birmingham City’s proposed Sports Quarter Stadium was also named in the UK’s bid, with plans for a 62,000-capacity stadium unveiled last year. Chelsea are exploring whether to expand Stamford Bridge or move to a new home in Earl’s Court, with their development also included in the UK’s bid.

As for existing stadiums in England, Aston Villa’s Villa Park, Brighton’s Amex Stadium, Bristol City’s Ashton Gate, Leeds United’s Elland Road, Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, Manchester City’s Etihad Stadium, Newcastle’s St James’ Park, Sunderland’s Stadium of Light and Nottingham Forest’s City Ground add to an ambitious list of venues.

Industry observers note that there are four further London venues on the list: Wembley, which could also host the final, Arsenal’s Emirates Stadium, Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park and the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Cardiff City’s Cardiff City Stadium and Wrexham’s Racecourse Ground are named, while Hampden Park in Glasgow, Easter Road in Edinburgh and Windsor Park in Belfast complete the proposed venues.

The final list of host cities and venues would be confirmed by Fifa closer to the start of the tournament, but the UK’s bid team said that 63 million people live within two hours of a proposed venue, making the World Cup the “most accessible tournament ever”.

By the time of the 2035 World Cup, many of the England players who played such an important role in the rise of women’s football by winning the Euros at Wembley in 2022 and becoming role models for the next generation will have likely hung up their boots.

Given that Lucy Bronze appears determined to appear at another major tournament for England next summer at the age of 35, it is not inconceivable that a 33-year-old Lauren James, or a 34-year-old Hannah Hampton, or a 35-year-old Lauren Hemp, or a 36-year-old Alessia Russo could still be representing the Lionesses by then.

But it is far more likely that the majority of the Lionesses squad for the World Cup, a tournament they have yet to win, will be built from players who are only just coming through the England pathway now and are at the moment representing teams from the Under-17s to the Under-23s.

Sarina Wiegman revealed she was excited about the potential of the next generation when naming her latest England squad last week. Midfielder Erica Meg Parkinson, 18, has kept her place after making her debut last month, while Chelsea’s Lexi Potter, 20, has also enjoyed a breakout year.

According to recent reports, “Hopefully these talents go from high potential to world-class players,” Wiegman said. “While I’m talking about that, I’m getting excited. It does excite me. I hope I have a contribution to that, but it starts with the players themselves.”.

In a recent development, after the initial wave brought through by the Lionesses, the next generation also now have a major target to aim for with a home World Cup in 2035. It could be game-changing for player development, while current stars such as Maya Le Tissier and Michelle Agyemang will look to further solidify their place in the England set-up in the years to come.

Recent findings suggest that “The thought of another generation growing up knowing that the biggest stage in the game is coming to their home country is amazing,” Agyemang stated. “To have the chance to play in a home World Cup would be a dream, but even more exciting is thinking about all the girls watching who might see 2035 and believe they can be part of it one day.”.

One of the most pivotal figures in English football over the last decade has been Wiegman, who led the Lionesses to three consecutive major tournament finals with her run as a manager stretching to five when you include previous achievements with the Netherlands. The FA recently declared that Wiegman had extended her contract with England through to the end of Euro 2029, which will mean she had been in the job for eight years. “I tend to think that’s the end point, but you never know,” Wiegman said when asked if she could stay beyond 2029. “I don’t strategy that far ahead. So let’s see where it gets to.”.

According to recent reports, wiegman will leave enormous shoes to fill when she eventually leaves England and the task of replacing one of the best coaches in the game is a sizeable one for the FA, but there is presently no obvious succession proposal. The FA should be able to produce up-and-coming English coaches as well as players, but all the top jobs in the Women’s Super League are filled by foreign managers.

Recent findings suggest that however, two attractive candidates could emerge in the shape of former England international Casey Stoney, who is now in charge of Canada, while Emma Hayes, after a decade at Chelsea, is preparing to lead the United States into next summer’s World Cup. Whether they could be available in future years depends on how they perform in the next two cycles. But knowing England will be hosts of the 2035 World Cup heightens the need for the FA to strategy for life after Wiegman, too.

The hope for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has to be that the World Cup can act as a catalyst for the growth of women’s football at home, in the same way as the Lionesses winning the Euros at Wembley in 2022 did for England.

In terms of grassroots participation and the development of domestic leagues, England’s victory four years ago was a boost for the other home nations, too, but nothing compares to the feeling of staging games in front of a nation on home soil.

Sources indicate that the tournament could be transformative, especially when you consider that the other home nations cannot take playing in major tournaments for granted. Scotland have only appeared at a Women’s World Cup once, in 2019, while Wales made history by qualifying for their first major tournament when they reached Euro 2025 and Northern Ireland did the same when they made it through to Euro 2022.

“Wales has been a football nation for 150 years and we have never hosted anything on this scale,” remarked Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales. “World Cup football played here, in front of Welsh children, would change what this game looks like in Wales: in the clubs, in the schools, and in the number of girls who grow up seeing a pathway into it.”.

Recent findings suggest that “A Women’s World Cup in Northern Ireland would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country,” the Irish Football Association’s chief executive Patrick Nelson said. “Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that.”.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the World Cup would be “the most significant thing to happen to the women’s and girls’ game in Scotland”. He added: “The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come.”.

Recent findings suggest that the announcement of the Women’s World Cup hosts was made by Fifa president Gianni Infantino, who lost the support of the English FA, Scottish FA, Welsh FA and Irish FA following his scrapped World Cup sell-off blueprint earlier this year. The FA chair, Debbie Hewitt, recently confirmed that they considered launching a legal challenge to Infantino’s eligibility to stand for a fourth term as Fifa president, highlighting the delicate politics that were at play while the bid for the 2035 Women’s World Cup was considered.

Industry observers note that infantino is standing for re-election in March and, under current rules, would be ineligible to run for a fifth term from 2031. Infantino should therefore be out of the picture by the time the UK hosts the World Cup in 2035, but they will have at least four years of working together on the World Cup if the Fifa president win his re-election bid. Infantino retains the support of the majority of Fifa’s member associations, but it’s a different story in the UK and prime minister Andy Burnham has previously called for his resignation.

There is already one area that could lead to some friction between the UK government and Fifa. The home nations’ bid received a score of 4.3 out of five in Fifa’s evaluation report. All but one of the categories – which include stadiums, transport and sustainability – were deemed “low risk” but the exception was “contractual framework”, with Fifa’s report stating “certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security”.

The Guardian has reported that Fifa has demanded tax-free status from ticket sales and broadcast and commercial partnerships, something that the UK government has not allowed when previously hosting major events such as the 2012 Olympics and will not offer to Uefa when they stage Euro 2028. The Independent reported extensively on the huge cost many US cities faced by hosting men’s World Cup matches last summer, and the UK will be keen to ensure that it will not face similar shortfalls in nine years’ time.

The 2035 World Cup will now act as the cornerstone for transforming football for women and girls in the UK, with the government working with the football associations from the four countries on three areas: making the game more accessible to girls and under-represented communities, developing coaching, officiating and leadership, and attracting more investment into women’s football.

A joint statement from the chief executives of the four associations mentioned: “What follows now is eight and a half years of work; on facilities, on coaching, on officiating, on the pathways that take a girl from her first game to a professional contract. The players who will light up 2035 are in our parks and playgrounds right now.”.

Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.
  • Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

Industry News: Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.
  • Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.
  • "Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

In a recent development, "Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp remarked, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves.".

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

Sources indicate that "I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp stated after the Netherlands match.

Recent findings suggest that "We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired.".

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

Recent findings suggest that but Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

In a recent development, scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

It has been revealed that "A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong.".

In a recent development, proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer.".

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

According to recent reports, "We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it.".

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

It has been revealed that in Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Fully 36 years after that legendary ‘bed-in’, a group of football supporters chose an equally unlikely venue to kick-start their own revolution.
